where: Section 2, last paragraph (why the theorem fails for thick plates and shafts)
problem: The direction of the thickness contribution is reversed. Writing Ix = ∫(y²+z²)dV, Iy = ∫(x²+z²)dV and Iz = ∫(x²+y²)dV, the out-of-plane material adds 2∫z²dV to Ix + Iy and adds nothing to Iz. So the sum fails because Ix + Iy is bigger than Iz, not because the material adds to Iz. The chapter says the opposite.
fix: Do not use this on a thick plate or a long shaft. There, an element at a distance z from the middle plane adds z² to Ix and to Iy, but nothing to the polar second moment about the normal axis. So Ix + Iy comes out larger than J and the theorem fails.

problem: The answer gives the same reversed reason (length material contributing to the polar moment but not to the in-plane moments). For a body of length along z, the polar moment about the length axis is ∫(x²+y²)dV and carries no z² term, while Ix and Iy each carry a z² term. The stated reason is wrong even though 'larger' / 'theorem fails' is the right conclusion.
fix: The shaft is not a thin flat area. Material far from the middle plane sits at distance z from it, so it adds z² to each of Ix and Iy but adds nothing to the polar second moment about the shaft axis. Then Ix + Iy is larger than J, so the theorem fails.

problem: The rectangle is given only as '40 mm by 60 mm' with no statement of which side lies along x, yet the answer assigns Ix = 40 × 60³/12. A student cannot tell which axis is x.
fix: Say 'a thin rectangle with the 40 mm side along x and the 60 mm side along y', or add that the polar value J is the same whichever side is called x.
